title: I'm from Indonesia
title_target: Я из Индонезии — Ya iz Indonezii
goal: Say where you're from, give your nationality and home city, and meet for the first time a noun ending that changes because of a preposition.
bekal: give your nationality in the right form for a man or a woman
name countries and cities in Russian
use the preposition из with a changing noun ending

dialogs.title: Диалог — In the registration queue
dialogs.intro: Day two of the course. Ani is queuing at the registration desk with another student, Марко. Notice that the country names change their endings as soon as из comes before them.

lines.speaker: Марко:
lines.id: Excuse me, do you study here too?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Yes. My name is Ani. Where are you from?
lines.literal: yes. me — they-call — Ani. from-where — you?

lines.speaker: Марко:
lines.id: I'm from Italy, from Milan. I'm Italian. And you?
lines.literal: I — from — Italy. from — Milan. I — Italian (m). and — you?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: I'm from Indonesia. I'm Indonesian (a woman).

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Because I'm a woman! You're an italyanets, your sister is an italyanka.
lines.literal: because — that — I — woman! you — Italian-man, your — sister — Italian-woman.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Hard, but interesting. Do you speak Russian?
lines.literal: difficult, but — interesting. you — speak — in-Russian?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Yes, well. And Indonesian, of course.

notes: **Nationality changes with the sex of the PERSON.** ⚠️ This is a classic mistake for English speakers, whose "Indonesian" or "Italian" fits everyone. In Russian a woman **cannot** call herself индонезиец. The pattern is tidy: the male form + **-ка** for a woman. *итальянец → итальян**ка***, *американец → американ**ка***, *японец → япон**ка***.

**The name of the language and the nationality are two different words.** *Я индонезийка* (I'm Indonesian) but *Я говорю по-индонезийски* (I speak Indonesian). The **по-…-ски** form is actually an adverb — literally "in a Russian way", "in an English way". It never changes, so once you know the pattern, every language is done at once.

**Из means "from", and the word after it MUST change its ending.** This is your first encounter with case. Индонези**я** → из Индонези**и**. Итали**я** → из Итали**и**. Москв**а** → из Москв**ы**. After из the noun is never left in its dictionary form.

**Why Милана, not Милан?** Masculine cities change too: Милан → из Милан**а**, Лондон → из Лондон**а**. Only foreign names that can't take endings stay put — and Джакарта is not one of them: из Джакарт**ы**. The truly rigid names are the ones ending in a foreign-sounding vowel: из Токио, из Осло.
**Почему asks "why", потому что answers "because".** They're a pair and almost always come one after the other. ⚠️ Notice that что in потому что is also said *shto*.
**Конечно is pronounced ka-NYESH-na.** The second word — after что — where ч sounds like *sh*. After these two, you can assume ч always sounds *ch*.
**Тоже means "too, also".** It moves around, but most often comes right after the word it adds to: *Вы **тоже** здесь учитесь?* — Do you study here too?

grammars.title: Из + genitive — your first case
body: After the preposition **из** (from), a noun moves into the genitive case. For now just learn the three ending patterns; you can forget the name for the moment.

head: Dictionary form
After из
Full example
rows: Я из Росси**и**. Я из Индонези**и**.
Я из Милан**а**. Я из Лондон**а**.

after: In speech, **из** often sounds like *is*: *из Италии* → *i-si-TA-li-i*. You're not mishearing; з really does lose its voice before a voiceless sound.
⚠️ Don't be tempted to use **от** for "from". От also means "from", but for **people**, not places: *письмо от мамы* (a letter from Mom). For where you come from, always из.

grammars.title: The country, its people and its language
body: Three columns for each country. The one you'll need most often in this course is in the top row.
after: ⚠️ **русский** breaks the pattern: it's an adjective, not a noun, so the female form is **русская** (not русскийка). The rest of the list follows the -ец / -ка pattern.
Unlike in English, nationalities are **not** capitalized in Russian: *я индонезийка*, not *я Индонезийка*. Only country names get a capital letter.

sections.title: Asking where someone is from, three levels deep

blocks.text: The "where are you from" question has three levels, and Russians usually work down them one by one in a first conversation.

head: Question
Say it
Asks
rows: the same, more casual word order

blocks.title: Two answers that always work
items: **Я из Индонезии.** — a safe answer for anyone, anywhere.

**Я из Индонезии, из Джакарты.** — answers the city too, and almost always invites the next question. Russians generally know Bali far better than Jakarta; *Вы знаете Бали? Это Индонезия.* is a sentence that opens many conversations.
⚠️ Don't answer *Я Индонезия* — that means "I am the country of Indonesia". The correct answers are **Я из Индонезии** (from) or **Я индонезийка** (the person).

exercises.prompt: Change the place name to its form after из.
Write the right nationality form for the person in brackets.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: России — Москвы — Индонезии — Лондона — Джакарты — Италии
Откуда вы? — Я из Индонезии. — Я немного говорю по-русски. — Русский язык трудный. — Я индонезийка.
Откуда вы? — Я из России, из Москвы. — Она итальянка. — Я немного говорю по-русски. — Русский язык трудный, но интересный. — Почему? Потому что я женщина.
